source_text: Quaesisti proxime, Fabi frater, fugiendum necne sit in persecutione, quod nescio quid annuntiaretur. Ibidem ego oblocutus aliquid pro loco ac tempore, et quarumdam personarum importunitate, semitractatam materiam abstuli mecum, plenius eam de stylo nunc renuntiaturus, utpote quam mihi et tua consultatio commendarat, et conditio temporum suo jam nomine injunxerat. Quanto enim frequentiores imminent persecutiones, tanto examinatio procuranda est, quomodo eas excipere fides debeat. Procuranda autem examinatio penes vos, qui, si forte, Paracletum non recipiendo deductorem omnis veritatis, merito adhuc etiam aliis quaestionibus obnoxii estis. Igitur consultationi tuae ordinem quoque induimus, animadvertentes ante determinari oportere de statu ipsius persecutionis, utrum a Deo obveniat, an a diabolo, quo facilius de obitu ejus constare possit. Omnis enim rei inspectio, auctore cognito, planior. Satis est quidem praescribere nihil fieri sine Dei voluntate. Sed non statim hac sententia caeteris retractatibus locum dabimus, ne a praesenti articulo avocemur, si quis responderit: Ergo et malum a Deo, et delictum a Deo; nihil jam in diabolo, nihil etiam in nobis ipsis. De persecutione nunc quaeritur. Circa hanc interim dixerim nihil fieri sine Dei voluntate, respiciens eam in primis dignam Deo esse, et, ut ita dixerim, necessariam, ad probationem scilicet servorum ejus sive reprobationem. Quis est enim exitus persecutionis, quis effectus alius, nisi probatio et reprobatio fidei, qua suos utique Dominus examinavit? Hoc omne judicium est persecutio per quam quis aut probatus aut reprobatus judicatur. Porro judicium soli Deo competit. Haec pala illa, quae et nunc Dominicam aream purgat, Ecclesiam scilicet, confusum acervum fidelium eventilans, frumentum martyrum et paleas negatorum. Haec enim, scalae quas somniat Jacob, aliis ascensum in superiora, aliis descensum ad inferiora demonstrantes. Sic et agonem intelligi capit persecutionem. A quo certamen edicitur, nisi a quo corona et praemia proponuntur? Legis edictum agonis istius in Apocalypsi, quibus praemiis ad victoriam invitet, vel maxime illos qui proprie vicerint in persecutione, vincendo luctati, revera non adversus carnem et sanguinem, sed adversus spiritalia nequitiae. Ita agnosces ad eumdem agonothetam pertinere certaminis arbitrium, qui invitat ad praemium. Totum quod agitur in persecutione, gloria Dei est probantis et reprobantis, imponentis et deponentis. Quod autem ad gloriam Dei pertinet, utique ex voluntate illius eveniet. Sed quando Deus magis creditur, nisi cum magis timetur, nisi in tempore persecutionis? Tunc Ecclesia in attonito est; tunc et fides in expeditione sollicitior et disciplinatior in jejuniis et stationibus, et orationibus, et humilitate, in alterutra diligentia et dilectione, in sanctitate et sobrietate. Non enim vacatur nisi timori et spei. Adeo et ex hoc ipso ostenditur nobis non posse diabolo deputari eam, quae meliores efficit Dei servos. Si quod iniquitas a Deo non est, sed a diabolo, persecutio autem ex iniquitate consistit (quid enim iniquius quam veri Dei antistites, omnis sectatores veritatis, nocentissimorum more tractari?), ideo videtur persecutio a diabolo evenire, a quo iniquitas agitur, ex qua constat persecutio: seire debemus, quatenus nec persecutio est sine iniquitate diaboli, nec probatio fidei sine persecutione, propter probationem fidei necessariam iniquitatem, non patrocinium praestare persecutioni, sed ministerium; praecedere enim Dei voluntatem circa fidei probationem, quae est ratio persecutionis, sequi autem diaboli iniquitatem ad instrumentum persecutionis, quae ratio est probationis. Nam et alias, in quantum justitiae iniquitas aemula est, in tantum materia est ad testimonia ejus, cujus est aemula; ut sic justitia in iniquitate perficiatur, quomodo virtus in infirmitate perficitur. Nam infirma mundi electa sunt a Deo, ut confundantur fortia; et stulta ejus, ut confundantur sapientia. Ita et iniquitas adhibetur ut justitia probetur, confundens iniquitatem. Igitur quod ministerium non est arbitrii, sed servitii (arbitrium enim Domini, persecutio, propter fidei probationem, ministerium autem iniquitas diaboli, propter persecutionis instructionem); ita eam per diabolum, si forte, non a diabolo evenire credimus. Nihil Satanae in servos Dei vivi licebit, nisi permiserit Dominus, ut aut ipsum destruat per fidem electorum in tentatione victricem: aut homines ejus fuisse traducat, qui defecerint ad illum. Habes exemplum Job, cui diabolus nullam potuit incutere tentationem, nisi a Deo accepisset potestatem, nec in substantiam quidem ejus, nisi Dominus, Ecce, dixisset, omnia quae sunt ei, in manu tua do, in ipsum autem ne extenderis manum. Denique nec extendit, nisi posteaquam et hoc postulanti Dominus, Ecce, dixisset, trado tibi illum, tantum animam ejus custodi. Sic et in Apostolos facultatem tentationis postulavit, non habens eam nisi ex permissu. Siquidem Dominus in Evangelio ad Petrum: Ecce, inquit, postulavit Satanas uti cerneret vos velut frumentum: verum ego rogavi pro te, ne deficeret fides tua: id est, ne tantum diabolo permitteretur, ut fides periclitaretur. Quo ostenditur, utrumque apud Deum esse, et concussionem fidei, et protectionem, cum utrumque ab eo petitur, concussio a diabolo, protectio a Filio. Et utique cum Filius Dei protectionem fidei habet in sua potestate quam a Patre postulat, a quo omnem accipit potestatem in coelis et in terris, quale est ut concussionem fidei diabolus in manu sua habeat? Sed in legitima Oratione cum dicimus ad Patrem: Ne nos inducas in tentationem (quae aut major tentatio quam persecutio?); ab eo illam profitemur accidere, a quo veniam ejus deprecamur: hoc est enim quod sequitur: Sed erue nos a maligno; id est, ne nos induxeris in tentationem, permittendo nos maligno. Tunc enim eruimur diaboli manibus, cum illi non tradimur in tentationem. Nec in porcorum gregem diaboli legio habuit potestatem, nisi eam de Deo impetrasset, tantum abest ut in oves Dei habeat. Possum dicere, porcorum quoque setas tunc numeratas apud Deum fuisse; nedum capillos sanctorum. Habere videtur diabolus propriam jam potestatem, si forte in eos qui ad Deum non pertinent, semel in stillam situtae, et in pulverem areae, et in salivam nationibus deputatis a Deo, ac per hoc diabolo expositis in vacuam quodammodo possessionem. Caeterum, in domesticos Dei nihil illi licet ex propria potestate; quia quando liceat, id est, ex quibus caussis, exempla in Scripturis signata demonstrant. Aut enim ex caussa probationis conceditur ei jus tentationis provocato vel provocanti, ut in superioribus: aut ex caussa reprobationis traditur ei peccator quasi carnifici in poenam, ut Saul: Et abscessit, inquit, spiritus Domini a Saule, et concutiebat eum spiritus nequam a Domino, et suffocabat. Aut ex caussa cohibitionis, ut Apostolus refert datum sibi sudem angelum Satanae ut colaphizetur: nec hanc speciem permitti diabolo in sanctos humiliandos per carnis vexationem, nisi simul ut et virtus tolerantiae scilicet in infirmitate perfici possit; nam et ipse Apostolus Phigellum et Hermogenem tradidit Satanae, uti emendentur, ne blasphement. Vides jam et a servis Dei facilius diabolum accipere potestatem, tanto abest ut eam ex proprietate possideat. Cum ergo et haec exempla magis in persecutionibus eveniant, siquidem magis tunc probamur vel reprobamur, et magis tunc humiliamur vel emendamur, ab eo permittatur vel imperetur necesse est catholice fieri haec, a quo et ex parte, scilicet ab illo qui dicit: Ego sum qui facio pacem, et condo mala, id est bellum. Hoc est enim contrarium paci. Nostrae autem paci quid est bellum, quam persecutio? Si persecutionis vel maxime exitus aut vitam afferunt aut mortem, aut plagam aut sanationem, habes auctorem ejusdem: Ego percutiam, et sanabo; ego vivificabo, et mortificabo. Uram, inquit, illos, sicut uritur argentum; et probabo, inpuid, illos, sicut probatur aurum. Cum enim exurimur persecutionis ardore, tunc probamur de fidei tenore. Haec erunt ignea jacula diaboli, per quae fidei ustio et conflatio administratur; ex Dei tamen voluntate. De isto quis dubitare possit ignoro, nisi plane frivola et frigida fides, deprehendens eos qui timide conveniunt in Ecclesiam. Dicitis enim, Quoniam incondite convenimus, simul convenimus, et complures concurrimus in Ecclesiam, quaerimur a nationibus, et timemus ne turbentur nationes. Annon scitis quod Deus omnium sit Dominus? Et si velit Deus, tunc persecutionem patieris; si vero noluerit, silebunt nationes. Credas utique; si tamen in eum Deum credis, sine cujus voluntate nec passer unius assis cadit in terram. Nos autem, puto, multis passeribus antistamus. Igitur si constat a quo persecutio eveniat, possumus jam consultationem tuam inducere, et determinare ex hoc ipso praetractatu, fugiendum in persecutione non esse. Si enim persecutio a Deo evenit, nullo modo fugiendum erit quod a Deo evenit. Sicut duplex ratio defendit, quia neque debeat devitari, neque evadi possit quod a Deo evenit. Non debet devitari, quia bonum. Necesse est enim bonum esse omne quod Deo visum est. Et numquid ideo in Genesi sic positum est: Et vidit Deus quia bonum est; non quod ignoraret bonum esse, nisi vidisset; sed ut hoc sono portenderet bonum esse, quod Deo visum est? Multa quidem sunt, quae a Deo eveniant, et alicujus malo eveniant. Imo bonum est ideo, quia a Deo evenit, ut divinum et rationale. Quid enim divinum non rationale, non bonum? Quid bonum non divinum? Si autem sensui cujusque videtur, non sensus hominis praejudicat statui, sed status sensui. Status enim uniuscujusque certum quid est, et dat sensui legem, ita sentiendi statum, sicuti est. Si autem statu quidem bonum quod a Deo venit (nihil enim a Deo non bonum, quia divinum, quia rationale), sensui vero malum videtur, erit status in tuto, sensus in vitio. Statu optima res pudicitia, et veritas, et justitia, quae a multorum sensu displicent. Nunquid ideo status sensui addicitur? Ita et persecutio statu bona est, quia divina et rationalis dispositio; sensui eorum vero quorum malo venit, displicet. Vides etiam illud malum rationem apud Deum habere, cum quis in persecutione evertitur de salute, sicut et illud bonum ratione contingere, cum quis ex persecutione proficit in salute? Nisi si irrationaliter quis aut perit apud Dominum, aut salvus est: is non poterit persecutionem malum dicere, quae etiam in mali parte bonum est, dum ratione administratur. Ita si bonum persecutio quoquo modo, quia de statu constat, merito definimus, quod bonum est, vitari non oportere: quia delictum sit, quod bonum est recusare; eo amplius, quod Deo visum est: jam vero nec posse vitari, quia a Deo evenit, cujus voluntas non poterit evadi. Igitur qui putant fugiendum, aut malum exprobrant Deo, si persecutionem uti malum fugiant; bonum enim nemo devitat; aut fortiores se Deo existimant, qui putant se evadere posse, si Deus tale aliquid voluerit evenire. Sed, Quod meum est, inquit, fugio, ne peream si negavero;
pass_a_gloss: You asked recently, brother Fabius, whether one should flee in persecution, because something was being announced, I do not know what. There I spoke something in that place and at that time, and because of the importunity of certain people, I took away with me a half-treated subject, which I am now going to explain more fully from my writing, as your consultation and the condition of the times had already commended it to me. For as much as persecutions are more frequent, so much more must the examination be procured, how faith should receive them. The examination to be procured is with you, who, if perhaps you do not receive the Paraclete, the guide of all truth, are still liable to other questions. Therefore, we are introducing order into your consultation, noticing that first it must be determined about the state of persecution itself, whether it comes from God or from the devil, so that it may be easier to be consistent about its occurrence. For every examination of a thing is clearer when the author is known. It is enough to prescribe that nothing happens without God's will. But we will not immediately give place to this opinion, retracting the other points, lest we be called away from the present article, if someone responds: Therefore, evil is also from God, and sin is from God; now there is nothing in the devil, nothing even in us ourselves. Now the question is about persecution. Concerning this, I will say in the meantime that nothing happens without God's will, considering that it is especially worthy of God and, so to speak, necessary for the testing of his servants or their rejection. For what is the outcome of persecution, what other effect, except the testing and rejection of faith, by which the Lord has certainly examined his own? This whole judgment is persecution, through which someone is judged either approved or rejected. Furthermore, judgment belongs to God alone. These are the winnowing fans that now purify the Lord's threshing floor, namely the Church, winnowing the confused heap of the faithful, the wheat of martyrs and the chaff of deniers. For these are the ladders that Jacob dreamed of, showing to some the ascent to higher things, to others the descent to lower things. Thus, persecution can also be understood as a contest. From whom is the contest announced, if not from him who offers the crown and the prizes? The edict of this contest is in the Apocalypse, with what prizes it invites to victory, especially those who have properly conquered in persecution, having struggled and won, truly not against flesh and blood, but against the spiritual forces of wickedness. So you will recognize that the judgment of the contest belongs to the same one who invites to the prize. Everything that happens in persecution is the glory of God, who tests and rejects, who appoints and deposes. But what pertains to the glory of God certainly happens by his will. But when is God more believed, if not when he is more feared, if not in the time of persecution? Then the Church is in astonishment; then faith is more solicitous and disciplined in fasts and stations, and prayers, and humility, in diligence and love, in sanctity and sobriety. For it is not idle except for fear and hope. So even from this it is shown to us that it cannot be attributed to the devil, what makes God's servants better. If something is not from God, but from the devil, and persecution consists of injustice (for what is more unjust than that the priests of the true God, all followers of truth, are treated like the most wicked?), therefore it seems that persecution happens from the devil, from whom injustice is done, from which persecution consists: we must know that persecution is not without the devil's injustice, nor is the testing of faith without persecution, because of the necessary injustice for the testing of faith, not to offer patronage to persecution, but ministry; for the will of God precedes concerning the testing of faith, which is the reason for persecution, but the devil's injustice follows for the instrument of persecution, which is the reason for testing. For also in other things, inasmuch as injustice is the rival of justice, it is to that extent the material for the testimonies of the one whose rival it is, so that justice may be perfected in injustice, just as virtue is perfected in weakness. For the weak things of the world have been chosen by God to confound the strong, and the foolish things, to confound the wise. So also injustice is used to prove justice, confounding injustice. Therefore, what is not the ministry of will, but of service (for the will of the Lord is persecution, for the testing of faith, the ministry, but the injustice of the devil, for the instruction of persecution); thus we believe that it happens through the devil, if perhaps, not from the devil. Nothing will be permitted to Satan against the living servants of God, except what the Lord permits, so that either he may destroy him through the victorious faith of the elect in temptation, or he may hand over those who have defected to him. You have the example of Job, to whom the devil was not able to bring any temptation, except what he had received power from God, nor even into his substance, except what the Lord had said, Behold, everything that he has is in your hand, but do not extend your hand against him. Finally, he did not extend it, except after the Lord had said to him who was asking, Behold, I deliver him to you, but keep his life. So also with the Apostles, he asked for the power of temptation, not having it except by permission. Indeed, the Lord in the Gospel to Peter: Behold, Satan has asked to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail, that is, that it may not be permitted to the devil to the extent that faith is endangered. By which it is shown that both the shaking of faith and its protection are with God, since both are asked from him, the shaking from the devil, the protection from the Son. And certainly, when the Son of God has the protection of faith in his power, which he asks from the Father, from whom he receives all power in heaven and on earth, what kind of thing is it that the devil has the shaking of faith in his hand? But in the legitimate Prayer, when we say to the Father: Do not lead us into temptation (what greater temptation than persecution?); we profess that it happens from him, from whom we beg for its forgiveness: for this is what follows: But deliver us from the evil one, that is, do not lead us into temptation, by permitting us to the evil one. For then we are delivered from the hands of the devil, when we are not handed over to him in temptation. Nor did the legion of the devil have power over the herd of swine, except what it had obtained from God, so much less does it have power over the sheep of God. I can say that even the bristles of the swine were then numbered before God; how much more the hairs of the saints. The devil seems to have his own power, if perhaps in those who do not belong to God, once they are given over to him, and to the dust of the threshing floor, and to the saliva of the nations, assigned by God, and thus exposed to the devil in a kind of empty possession. Nevertheless, in the servants of God, nothing is permitted to him from his own power; because when it is permitted, that is, from what causes, the examples marked in the Scriptures demonstrate. For either the right of temptation is granted to him because of the cause of testing, provoked or provoking, as in the above; or because of the cause of rejection, the sinner is handed over to him like an executioner for punishment, as Saul: And the spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him, and suffocated him. Or because of the cause of restraint, as the Apostle reports, a thorn was given to him, an angel of Satan to buffet him; nor is this kind of thing permitted to the devil in the saints, to humble them through the vexation of the flesh, except at the same time so that the virtue of endurance may be perfected in weakness; for the Apostle himself handed over Phygellus and Hermogenes to Satan, that they might be corrected, lest they blaspheme. You see now that the devil more easily receives power from the servants of God, so much less does he possess it from his own property. When, therefore, these examples happen more in persecutions, since we are more tested or rejected then, and more humbled or corrected then, it is necessary that these things be permitted or commanded by God, from whom both the permission and the command come, namely from him who says: I am the one who makes peace, and creates evil, that is, war. For this is the opposite of peace. But what is war to our peace, except persecution? If the outcomes of persecution bring either life or death, either plague or healing, you have the author of it: I will strike, and I will heal; I will kill, and I will make alive. I will refine them, he says, like silver; and I will test them, like gold. For when we are refined by the fire of persecution, then we are tested by the quality of our faith. These will be the fiery darts of the devil, through which the burning and testing of faith are administered; but from God's will. I do not know who can doubt this, except perhaps those with a frivolous and cold faith, who are caught gathering timidly in the Church. For you say: Since we gather in disorder, and we gather together, and many of us come together in the Church, we are sought by the nations, and we fear lest the nations be disturbed. Do you not know that God is the Lord of all? And if God wills, then you will suffer persecution; but if he does not will, the nations will be silent. You should certainly believe; if, however, you believe in that God, without whose will not even a sparrow falls to the ground, and we, I think, are worth many sparrows. Therefore, if it is established from whom persecution comes, we can now introduce your consultation, and determine from this very preface that one should not flee in persecution. For if persecution comes from God, it will not be fled from in any way, because it comes from God. Just as the double reason defends, because neither should it be avoided, nor can it be evaded, what comes from God. It should not be avoided, because it is good. For it is necessary that everything that has been seen by God is good. And is it not so placed in Genesis: And God saw that it is good; not because he did not know that it is good, unless he had seen; but so that he might portend by this sound that it is good, what has been seen by God? Many things indeed happen from God, and happen for the sake of some evil. Indeed, it is good, because it happens from God, as something divine and rational. For what is divine is not rational, not good? What is good is not divine? If it seems to someone's sense, not the sense of man prejudges the state, but the state prejudges the sense. For the state of each thing is a certain thing, and gives the sense a law, so that it may be sensed in the state, as it is. But if the state is indeed good, what comes from God (for nothing comes from God that is not good, because it is divine, because it is rational), and it seems evil to the sense, the state will be in safety, the sense in error. The state is optimal in chastity, and truth, and justice, which are displeasing to the sense of many. Should the state therefore be subject to the sense? So also persecution is good in state, because it is a divine and rational disposition; but it is displeasing to the sense of those to whom it comes for evil. You see also that evil has a reason with God, when someone is overturned in salvation through persecution, just as also good happens with reason, when someone profits in salvation from persecution? Unless someone perishes or is saved irrationally before the Lord: he will not be able to say that persecution is evil, which is also good in the part of evil, while it is administered with reason. So if persecution is good in any way, because it is established from the state, we rightly define that what is good should not be avoided; because it is a fault to refuse what is good; all the more so, because it has been seen by God: now, indeed, it cannot be avoided, because it happens from God, whose will cannot be evaded. Therefore, those who think that one should flee, either reproach God with evil, if they flee from persecution as from evil; for no one avoids what is good; or they consider themselves stronger than God, who think they can evade it, if God wills something like this to happen. But, What is mine, he says, I flee, lest I perish if I deny;

pass_b_english: Brother Fabius, you recently asked whether one should flee during persecution, prompted by some unspecified rumor. At the time I spoke briefly, as the occasion and the crowd allowed, and I took the half-finished matter home to treat it more fully in writing, since both your inquiry and the signs of the times demanded it. The more frequent persecutions become, the more urgently we must determine how faith ought to receive them. That determination belongs to you—though if you happen to reject the Paraclete, the guide into all truth, you remain liable to still more questions. So let us bring order to your inquiry, first settling the status of persecution itself: does it come from God or the devil? Knowing the author makes every examination clearer. It is true enough to say nothing happens without God's will, but we will not let that axiom shut down the rest of the argument prematurely, lest someone retort: 'Then evil comes from God, and sin from God; the devil has no role, and neither do we.' The question right now is persecution. I say provisionally that it does not happen without God's will, because it is preeminently worthy of him—indeed, necessary—for the testing of his servants or their rejection. What else is the outcome of persecution but the testing and rejection of faith, by which the Lord has always examined his own? Persecution is the whole judgment: through it a person is judged either approved or rejected. And judgment belongs to God alone. Persecution is the winnowing fork that now cleans the Lord's threshing floor—the Church—sifting the confused heap of the faithful into the wheat of martyrs and the chaff of deniers. These are the ladders Jacob dreamed of, showing some the ascent to higher things, others the descent to lower things (Genesis). Persecution can also be understood as a contest. Who announces the contest but the one who offers the crown and the prizes? The edict of this contest stands in the Apocalypse, listing the prizes that invite to victory—especially those who have properly conquered in persecution, struggling and winning, not against flesh and blood but against the spiritual forces of wickedness (Apocalypse). So you will recognize that the judging of the contest belongs to the same one who invites to the prize. Everything that happens in persecution is the glory of God, who tests and rejects, who appoints and deposes. What pertains to God's glory certainly happens by his will. When is God more believed than when he is more feared—if not in the time of persecution? Then the Church stands in awe; then faith becomes more solicitous and disciplined in fasts, vigils, prayers, humility, diligence and love, holiness and sobriety. There is leisure for nothing except fear and hope. This alone shows persecution cannot be credited to the devil, since it makes God's servants better. If injustice is not from God but from the devil, and persecution consists of injustice—what is more unjust than treating the priests of the true God, all followers of truth, like the worst criminals?—then persecution seems to come from the devil, from whom injustice proceeds. We must understand: persecution is not without the devil's injustice, nor is the testing of faith without persecution. The necessary injustice serves the testing of faith not as patronage of persecution but as its ministry; God's will precedes, ordaining the testing of faith as the reason for persecution, while the devil's injustice follows as the instrument of persecution, which is the reason for the testing. In other matters, too, insofar as injustice rivals justice, it serves as material for the testimonies of the one it rivals, so that justice is perfected in injustice, just as virtue is perfected in weakness. The weak things of the world God chose to shame the strong, the foolish to shame the wise. So injustice is used to prove justice, confounding injustice. Therefore this ministry is not of will but of service: the Lord's will is persecution, for the testing of faith; the ministry is the devil's injustice, for the execution of persecution. Thus we believe it happens through the devil, if at all—not from the devil. Nothing is permitted Satan against the living servants of God except what the Lord allows, either to destroy the devil through the victorious faith of the elect in temptation, or to hand over those who have defected to him. You have the example of Job: the devil could inflict no temptation on him except what he received power from God to do, nor even touch his substance, until the Lord said, 'Behold, all he has is in your hand, but do not lay a hand on him.' Finally he did not lay a hand on him until the Lord said to the one asking, 'Behold, I deliver him to you; only spare his life' (Genesis). So also with the apostles, he asked for the power of temptation, possessing it only by permission. The Lord in the Gospel told Peter, 'Behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail'—that is, that it might not be permitted to the devil to the point that faith is endangered (Gospel). This shows both the shaking of faith and its protection are with God, since both are asked of him: the shaking by the devil, the protection by the Son. And when the Son of God holds the protection of faith in his power, which he asks from the Father, from whom he receives all authority in heaven and on earth, how could the devil hold the shaking of faith in his own hand? In the Lord's Prayer, when we say to the Father, 'Do not lead us into temptation'—what greater temptation than persecution?—we confess it comes from him from whom we beg deliverance: 'But deliver us from the evil one,' that is, do not lead us into temptation by handing us over to the evil one. For then we are snatched from the devil's hands, when we are not handed over to him in temptation. The legion of the devil had no power over the herd of swine except what it obtained from God; how much less over the sheep of God? I would say even the bristles of the swine were then numbered before God; how much more the hairs of the saints. The devil appears to have his own power only over those who do not belong to God—once given over to him, like chaff on the threshing floor, like spittle of the nations assigned by God, and thus exposed to the devil in a kind of vacant possession. But over God's household nothing is permitted him from his own authority; the scriptural examples show exactly when and why permission is granted. Either the right of temptation is granted him for the cause of testing, whether provoked or provoking, as above; or for the cause of rejection, the sinner is handed over to him like an executioner for punishment, as with Saul: 'The Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord tormented him'; or for the cause of restraint, as the apostle reports a thorn was given him, an angel of Satan to buffet him—not permitted to the devil among the saints to humble them through fleshly affliction unless at the same time the virtue of endurance might be perfected in weakness. The apostle himself handed Hymenaeus and Alexander over to Satan that they might be corrected, not blaspheme. You see now that the devil receives power more easily from the servants of God—so far is he from possessing it by right. Since these examples occur more in persecutions, when we are more tested or rejected, more humbled or corrected, they must be permitted or commanded by God, from whom both permission and command come—from him who says, 'I make peace and create evil, that is, war' (Isaiah). War is the opposite of peace; what is war to our peace but persecution? If the outcomes of persecution bring either life or death, wounding or healing, you have its author: 'I strike, and I heal; I kill, and I make alive.' 'I will refine them like silver, and test them like gold.' When we are refined by the fire of persecution, then we are tested by the quality of our faith. These are the fiery darts of the devil, through which the burning and testing of faith are administered—but from God's will. I do not know who could doubt this except a frivolous and cold faith, caught gathering timidly in the Church. You say, 'Because we gather disorderly, and we gather together, and many of us crowd into the Church, we are watched by the nations, and we fear lest the nations be disturbed.' Do you not know that God is Lord of all? If God wills, you will suffer persecution; if he does not will, the nations will be silent. You should believe this—if you believe in that God without whose will not even a sparrow falls to the ground, and we, I think, are worth many sparrows (Gospel). Therefore, if it is established from whom persecution comes, we can now proceed with your consultation and determine from this very preface that one should not flee in persecution. For if persecution comes from God, it must not be fled in any way, because it comes from God. A double reason defends this: what comes from God should not be avoided, and cannot be evaded. It should not be avoided because it is good. Everything that God has seen must be good. Is it not written in Genesis: 'And God saw that it was good'—not because he did not know it was good unless he saw it, but so that by this statement he might signal that what God sees is good (Genesis)? Many things happen from God and happen for someone's evil. Indeed, it is good because it comes from God, as something divine and rational. What is divine is not rational, not good? What is good is not divine? If it seems otherwise to someone's perception, the perception of man does not prejudge the state of things; the state prejudges the perception. The state of each thing is fixed and gives perception its law, so that it may perceive the state as it is. If the state is good—what comes from God (for nothing from God is not good, because divine, because rational)—but it seems evil to perception, the state stands secure, the perception is in error. Chastity, truth, justice are optimal in state, though displeasing to many perceptions. Should the state therefore be subjected to perception? So persecution is good in state, because it is a divine and rational disposition; it displeases only the perception of those to whom it comes for evil. You see that evil has its reason with God, when someone is ruined in salvation through persecution, just as good has its reason when someone profits in salvation from persecution? Unless someone perishes or is saved irrationally before the Lord, he cannot call persecution evil, which is good even in its evil aspect, because it is administered with reason. So if persecution is good in any way, because it is established by the state, we rightly define that what is good should not be avoided; it is a fault to refuse what is good—all the more because God has seen it. Nor can it be avoided, because it comes from God, whose will cannot be evaded. Therefore those who think one should flee either reproach God with evil, if they flee persecution as evil—no one avoids what is good—or they consider themselves stronger than God, thinking they can evade what God wills to happen. 'What is mine, I flee,' he says, 'lest I perish if I deny.'

review.notes: Pass A and Pass B both fail to correctly identify the names of the individuals mentioned in the Latin text. The Latin text says 'Phigellum et Hermogenem' (Phygellus and Hermogenes), but Pass B translates this as 'Hymenaeus and Alexander'. This is a significant error in identity/agency. Additionally, Pass B adds a scripture citation (Isaiah) to the clause 'Ego sum qui facio pacem, et condo mala, id est bellum' which is not present in the Locked Latin, though it is an allusion to Isaiah 45:7; however, the primary failure is the misidentification of the names.
reasons: Pass B misidentifies the names 'Phigellum et Hermogenem' as 'Hymenaeus and Alexander' (line: 'the apostle himself handed Hymenaeus and Alexander over to Satan').

review.notes: ["Quaesisti proxime, Fabi frater, fugiendum necne sit in persecutione, quod nescio quid annuntiaretur.", "Igitur consultationi tuae ordinem quoque induimus, animadvertentes ante determinari oportere de statu ipsius persecutionis, utrum a Deo obveniat, an a diabolo, quo facilius de obitu ejus constare possit.", "Omnis enim rei inspectio, auctore cognito, planior.", "Satis est quidem praescribere nihil fieri sine Dei voluntate.", "Non enim vacatur nisi timori et spei.", "Habes exemplum Job, cui diabolus nullam potuit incutere tentationem, nisi a Deo accepisset potestatem.", "Cum ergo et haec exempla magis in persecutionibus eveniant, siquidem magis tunc probamur vel reprobamur, et magis tunc humiliamur vel emendamur, ab eo permittatur vel imperetur necesse est catholice fieri haec, a quo et ex parte, scilicet ab illo qui dicit: Ego sum qui facio pacem, et condo mala, id est bellum.", "Si persecutionis vel maxime exitus aut vitam afferunt aut mortem, aut plagam aut sanationem, habes auctorem ejusdem: Ego percutiam, et sanabo; ego vivificabo, et mortificabo.", "Igitur qui putant fugiendum, aut malum exprobrant Deo, si persecutionem uti malum fugiant; bonum enim nemo devitat; aut fortiores se Deo existimant, qui putant se evadere posse, si Deus tale aliquid voluerit evenire.", "Quod meum est, inquit, fugio, ne peream si negavero;"]
